text: Every client script record on sys_script_client has an Isolate script checkbox. It's easy to skim past, but it decides where the script actually runs — either sandboxed off by itself, or sharing space with everything else on the page. This lesson is about what it actually does, and why most scripts in this course and in a real instance should leave it checked.

Here's Script A, not isolated, declaring a top-level variable called helperIndex and setting it inside onLoad. Because this script isn't isolated, that variable doesn't live in some private space just for this script — it lands directly in the page's shared global scope, the same scope the form itself and any UI Macros on the page also use.

Now here's Script B, written by a different developer in a completely different file, also not isolated, and it happens to use the exact same variable name, helperIndex, because that name felt locally obvious to write. Because both scripts share the same global scope, this isn't two separate variables — it's one, and Script B silently overwrites whatever Script A was tracking. Neither developer sees an error; the bug just shows up later as one script mysteriously breaking after the other was added, which is exactly the kind of failure that's miserable to trace.

With Isolate script checked on both, each one runs inside its own sandboxed iframe that the platform injects specifically to hold client script execution, so helperIndex in Script A and helperIndex in Script B never touch the same memory — the collision simply can't happen. The real exception is narrow: certain legacy UI Macro interactions or older integrations that genuinely need direct global-scope access, and those should be documented on the script itself, not assumed.

That's the one checkbox on every sys_script_client record that decides all of this. Checked, sandboxed and collision-proof, and also more stable and secure since other page script can't reach into it. Unchecked, sharing the page's global scope with everything else on it. The standing rule for this course, and for a real instance, is: isolate by default, and only uncheck it with a documented reason.
Lesson 10 puts all four client script types and isolation together in one real lab — an onCellEdit guard on the Incident list, and its isolated onChange twin enforcing the same rule on the form.
